claim: The selected stream is Doctor / Care Team Facing and the programme excludes diagnosis, treatment recommendations, clinical decision support, clinical risk scoring, interpretation of medical data, and autonomous clinical advice.
source_title: Health-a-thon design principles and scope
supporting_extract: The supplied official text lists the selected stream, six exclusions, human override, auditability, light integration, and assistive workflow expectations.
method_sample: Official programme rules captured from the programme site.
limitations: The live rules may change and must be rechecked before submission.
frequency_evidence: Not applicable; this is a programme constraint.
burden_evidence: Not applicable; this is a programme constraint.
current_workaround: Not applicable.
existing_solution: Not applicable.
contradiction: Official use-case wording sometimes mentions meaningful changes, but the stricter global exclusion on medical-data interpretation governs scope.
implication: Only operational assistance with human review is promotable.
unknowns: Exact boundary review is still required for each proposed capability.
provenance_notes: Primary local capture; exact exclusions preserved.

claim: The official consultation-readiness use case describes longitudinal reconstruction from notes, laboratory investigations, imaging, treatment records, medication history, scanned reports, PDFs, images, and patient-provided documents.
source_title: Health-a-thon 2026 — Consultation Readiness & Patient Journey Review
supporting_extract: Busy outpatient clinics leave little time for assembly; the desired direction includes diverse structured and unstructured inputs and visible missing or inconsistent information.
method_sample: Official programme use-case description.
limitations: An illustrative use case establishes programme fit, not observed prevalence or burden in a specific oncology setting.
frequency_evidence: Described as a recurring follow-up consultation problem; no rate reported.
burden_evidence: Administrative work and reduced patient interaction are stated; no measured time reported.
current_workaround: Manual reconstruction across systems and patient-provided documents.
existing_solution: Existing EMRs, labs, imaging systems, and manual records are named but not evaluated.
contradiction: The use case's broad language must be narrowed by the programme-wide ban on medical-data interpretation.
implication: Consultation preparation is strongly aligned, but only literal extraction, organisation, provenance, and human review are safe.
unknowns: Named preparer, oncology segment, frequency, time burden, and local existing-system gap.
provenance_notes: Programme direction, not workflow observation.

claim: Supplied clinician-derived notes report difficulty finding guidelines, publications, drug monographs, trials, toxicity criteria, staging information, interactions, and India-specific oncology information.
source_title: Oncologist Pain Points
supporting_extract: The notes group requests for faster source finding, India-specific information, guideline comparison, trial discovery, staging, toxicity, interactions, and clinical-tool access.
method_sample: Unknown number and type of clinician conversations; interview method and sample are not recorded.
limitations: No participant count, setting, frequency, severity, or verbatim attribution for most items; several requested functions cross the programme boundary.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Described as cumbersome or difficult; no measured time or operational result.
current_workaround: Searching fragmented professional sources and trial literature is implied.
existing_solution: Not evaluated in the supplied notes.
contradiction: Experienced oncologists may prefer authentic sources and established protocols over AI-generated treatment recommendations.
implication: Decompose general authentic-source retrieval from patient-specific CDS before evaluating product fit.
unknowns: Which searches recur, how long they take, who performs them, and why current sources are insufficient.
provenance_notes: Atomic summary of several rows from one underlying supplied source; must not count as multiple confirmations.

claim: The supplied notes say generic answers are insufficient and identify cancer, stage, biomarker, line of therapy, previous treatment, comorbidities, and specialty as relevant context dimensions.
source_title: Oncologist Pain Points
supporting_extract: The source explicitly separates context-specific information and specialty-specific medical, surgical, and radiation needs.
method_sample: Unknown number and type of clinician conversations.
limitations: The source does not distinguish safe record organisation from patient-specific clinical interpretation.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Clinicians apply context while searching multiple sources; details are not reported.
existing_solution: Not evaluated.
contradiction: Patient-specific contextual ranking can become prohibited clinical decision support.
implication: Use separate vocabulary for record contextualisation and clinical contextualisation.
unknowns: Which dimensions matter to one selected operational job and where each is recorded.
provenance_notes: Same underlying supplied research source as EV-0003; not independent confirmation.

claim: The supplied notes report that doctors want to upload reports in different formats and receive a concise view to reconstruct clinical history.
source_title: Oncologist Pain Points
supporting_extract: Patient information is described as fragmented across pathology, imaging, molecular information, and treatment history.
method_sample: Unknown number and type of clinician conversations.
limitations: No named workflow, preparer, frequency, measured burden, current system, trust requirement, or evaluation of summary review cost.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Need for quick reconstruction is asserted; no measurement reported.
current_workaround: Manual review of reports is implied.
existing_solution: Not evaluated.
contradiction: A generated summary can increase risk and verification work if it lacks exact provenance or introduces interpretation.
implication: Fragmentation is a priority research lane, but the product form must remain source-linked and clinician-reviewed.
unknowns: Primary actor, trigger, input set, workflow time, error modes, and existing alternative.
provenance_notes: Source claim only; concise summary wording is not adopted as a safe product requirement.

claim: The supplied notes include requests for dosing and dose modification, toxicity grading, drug-interaction checking, staging, indications, and trial availability.
source_title: Oncologist Pain Points
supporting_extract: The Act theme groups practical trusted information such as dose changes, toxicity grading, interactions, indications, trials, and guideline comparison.
method_sample: Unknown number and type of clinician conversations.
limitations: Requests are not quantified and many patient-specific forms are outside the official scope.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Described as cumbersome or needed quickly; no measurement reported.
current_workaround: Drug labels, monographs, guidelines, and literature are mentioned.
existing_solution: Not systematically evaluated.
contradiction: The official programme excludes medical-data interpretation, CDS, risk scoring, and treatment recommendations.
implication: Retain as need evidence but exclude patient-specific clinical functions from candidate promotion.
unknowns: Whether a valuable general-source retrieval or documentation workflow surrounds the prohibited task.
provenance_notes: Research finding retained explicitly as non-promotable clinical scope.

claim: One identified doctor in the supplied synthesis reportedly valued authentic sources, knowledge sharing, doubt clearing, clinical discussion, research, and presentation work more than AI treatment recommendations.
source_title: Oncologist Pain Points
supporting_extract: The source's stated opportunity is a trusted workspace for finding, synthesising, contextualising, and using information faster, not AI that tells oncologists what treatment to give.
method_sample: Single unidentified doctor account summarised by the source author.
limitations: One unidentified participant; no setting, frequency, or direct transcript; preference may not generalise.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Established protocols and authentic sources are preferred; details are not reported.
existing_solution: Not evaluated.
contradiction: Other supplied requests seek patient-specific clinical tools, showing that needs and safe hackathon scope do not fully overlap.
implication: Prioritise provenance and human knowledge exchange over generated clinical answers.
unknowns: How frequent the work is, which source types matter, and whether existing tools already satisfy it.
provenance_notes: Preserves the source's single-participant limitation.

claim: An informal supplied discussion describes patients carrying longitudinal records and retelling history from memory when a clinician lacks a quickly reviewable historical record.
source_title: Onco Grid chatroom notes
supporting_extract: The discussion raises patient-carried documents, repeated narration, missed details, heterogeneous hospital systems, and data-compliance concerns.
method_sample: Informal team discussion containing personal examples and unverified assertions.
limitations: Anecdotal, duplicated and truncated source text; includes ambiguous trust language and cannot establish oncology prevalence.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Missed details and repeated narration are asserted; no measured impact.
current_workaround: Patients carry records and narrate history.
existing_solution: Not evaluated.
contradiction: The example is not itself an observed oncology workflow and patients may maintain continuity with one oncologist.
implication: Use only to generate questions about intake and cross-provider records; do not generalise or publish raw notes.
unknowns: Prevalence, oncology-specific actors, trust process, consent, and the role of existing digital records.
provenance_notes: Sanitised paraphrase; no personal detail copied from the raw source.

claim: NCG/KCDO already publishes oncology EMR requirements, supports empanelled vendors and adoption, and is piloting an ABDM-based interoperability blueprint for structured and unstructured cancer data.
source_title: NCG/KCDO Oncology EMR initiative
supporting_extract: The initiative covers medical, surgical, radiation, and multidisciplinary workflows, dashboards, adoption support, empanelled vendors, and interoperability pilot testing.
method_sample: Official initiative and requirements page.
limitations: Describes intended capabilities and programme activity, not adoption quality or effectiveness in every hospital.
frequency_evidence: Not applicable to capability existence; adoption prevalence is not established by this page.
burden_evidence: The page cites EMR selection and implementation challenges but gives no measured workflow burden.
current_workaround: Hospitals select and implement EMRs with varying oncology capability.
existing_solution: NCG requirements, empanelled oncology EMRs, LEAP adoption support, dashboards, and interoperability work.
contradiction: Generic oncology EMR, dashboard, and longitudinal-record concepts are not blank-market opportunities.
implication: Candidate differentiation must target a validated last-mile gap that NCG-aligned systems do not already solve.
unknowns: Actual adoption, target-setting implementation quality, and remaining user workflow gaps.
provenance_notes: Official capability claim; effectiveness remains unverified.

claim: The draft ABDM FHIR Implementation Guide defines R4-based exchange artifacts and profiles including diagnostic reports, discharge summaries, health documents, outpatient consultations, prescriptions, encounters, observations, medications, procedures, and service requests.
source_title: FHIR Implementation Guide for ABDM v7.0.0
publisher: National Resource Centre for EHR Standards
supporting_extract: The guide identifies Health Information Provider and Health Information User actors and minimum exchange profiles for structured and unstructured health artifacts.
method_sample: Official local-development draft implementation guide based on FHIR R4.0.1.
limitations: Draft guide; technical capability does not prove implementation or oncology workflow fit.
frequency_evidence: Not applicable to a standard.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Not reported.
existing_solution: ABDM consent-based exchange architecture and profiles.
contradiction: A new proprietary universal data model may duplicate an evolving national interoperability direction.
implication: Use ABDM/FHIR as a reference and narrow adapter boundary, not a claimed phase-one production integration.
unknowns: Target hospital readiness, actual exchanged artifacts, consent workflow, and final v7 publication changes.
provenance_notes: Version and draft date captured exactly.

claim: The NCG/KCDO Medical Oncology Module defines connected requirements for protocol master, doctor notes, nurse notes, toxicity monitoring, on-treatment discharge summary, and completion summary.
source_title: NCG-KCDO EMR Requirement — Medical Oncology Module v2.0
supporting_extract: The module separates planned protocol, prescribing review, nursing administration, monitoring, treatment-course summary, and completion documentation.
method_sample: Official requirements developed by an NCG medical-oncology subcommittee using expertise and best-practice discussion.
limitations: Requirements and intended workflow, not an observation of adoption, usability, or burden in a specific hospital.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Not reported.
existing_solution: NCG-aligned oncology EMR modules can implement these connected records.
contradiction: A generic treatment timeline may duplicate existing structured EMR requirements and may cross into clinical interpretation.
implication: Research last-mile fragmented outside records and handoffs rather than rebuilding protocol or treatment-decision functions.
unknowns: Actual hospital adoption and where records still leave or enter the module manually.
provenance_notes: Requirements are not represented as observed practice.

claim: The NCG/KCDO Surgical Oncology Module defines requirements spanning operation-theatre booking and worklists, safety checks, surgery, anaesthesia, postoperative events, and reports.
source_title: NCG-KCDO EMR Requirement — Surgical Oncology Module v2.0
supporting_extract: The requirements expose cross-role preparation and documentation around theatre, surgery, anaesthesia, postoperative care, and reporting.
method_sample: Official specialty EMR requirements.
limitations: Intended capability, not measured implementation or burden.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Not reported.
existing_solution: NCG-aligned surgical oncology EMR requirements.
contradiction: Specialty workflow depth argues against one universal oncology summary.
implication: Cross-department readiness and record handoff may matter more than duplicating internal surgical workflow.
unknowns: Actual handoff failures, actors, frequency, and systems in target settings.
provenance_notes: Requirements are not represented as observed practice.

claim: The NCG/KCDO Radiation Oncology Module defines specialised requirements for common inputs, external-beam and brachytherapy planning and delivery, interruptions, monitoring, completion, and follow-up.
source_title: NCG-KCDO EMR Requirement — Radiation Oncology Module v2.0
supporting_extract: The module reflects specialised planning, delivery, interruption, monitoring, completion, and follow-up artifacts and roles.
method_sample: Official specialty EMR requirements.
limitations: Intended capability, not measured implementation or burden.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Not reported.
existing_solution: Specialised radiation oncology and treatment-planning systems plus NCG requirements.
contradiction: Radiation planning and dosimetry cannot be reduced to a generic longitudinal dashboard.
implication: Limit product research to operational inputs, handoffs, and source-linked completion records; never interpret or design a treatment plan.
unknowns: Where cross-system and outside-record gaps remain in actual institutions.
provenance_notes: Requirements are not represented as observed practice.

claim: The NCG/KCDO Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Module defines a case packet containing presentation, history and prior treatment, pathology and imaging attachments, question for the board, specialty comments, final human decision, and follow-up.
source_title: NCG-KCDO EMR Requirement — Multi Disciplinary Tumor Board Module v2.0
supporting_extract: The requirements separate case preparation, evidence attachments, the question, specialty inputs, final decision, and follow-up.
method_sample: Official multidisciplinary oncology EMR requirements.
limitations: Does not measure actual preparation burden, adoption, participation, or outcome.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Not reported.
existing_solution: NCG-aligned multidisciplinary tumour-board module requirements.
contradiction: A generic peer-discussion platform duplicates formal workflow unless it addresses a specific access or last-mile preparation gap.
implication: A source-linked reviewed case packet may support human discussion, but novelty and measurable burden remain unproven.
unknowns: Case-selection frequency, preparer role, missing inputs, time burden, non-metro access, and current tool adoption.
provenance_notes: Requirements are not represented as observed practice.

subproblem: Indian oncology EMR priority and adoption
claim: In a 2022 NCG member survey, 81 of 101 responding organisations prioritised EMRs; the NCG initiative then developed workflow-specific requirements and supported more than 20 centres with procurement and adoption.
source_title: National Cancer Grid initiative for electronic medical records, India
publisher: Bulletin of the World Health Organization
supporting_extract: The paper names inefficient workflows, incomplete data, retrieval difficulty, interoperability, documentation time, and clinician resistance to manual data entry as implementation problems.
method_sample: Implementation report; NCG network of more than 360 centres; requirements informed by a 101-respondent member survey, representative-centre assessment, clinician and IT interviews, and stakeholder consultation.
limitations: The 81-of-101 result measures organisational priority, not end-user burden; authors lead the initiative and adoption outcomes are not controlled effectiveness evidence.
frequency_evidence: 80% of 101 responding member organisations prioritised EMRs; response selection limits generalisation.
burden_evidence: Documentation time and resistance are reported but not quantified.
current_workaround: Existing hospital systems and manual data collection vary across centres.
existing_solution: Six NCG-aligned vendor products, modules, interoperability work, and adoption support.
contradiction: The breadth of existing NCG work weakens novelty claims for a generic oncology EMR or chronology view.
implication: Investigate a narrow last-mile gap and adoption condition rather than rebuilding existing requirements.
unknowns: Which supported centres adopted which workflows and what burden remains after implementation.
provenance_notes: Peer-reviewed implementation report; organisational priority and intended improvement are not treated as measured clinician outcomes.

claim: NCG/KCDO field research reports dual paper-and-online maintenance, redundant entry, fragmented information across computers, inability to view or upload prior referral details, slow systems, and workflows that do not match users' mental models.
source_title: UI/UX Guidelines for EMR & Clinical Systems
supporting_extract: The published audit lists 11 findings, including offline and online duplication, fragmented computers, referral-history access gaps, redundant patient records, excessive manual entry, and mobile-device preferences.
method_sample: Field research, user interviews, and UX audit with doctors, nurses, and administrative staff; sample size and site count are not reported in the document.
limitations: Healthcare-general rather than oncology-only; missing sample and site detail; design partner publication rather than independent evaluation.
frequency_evidence: Problems are presented as recurring audit findings; rates are not reported.
burden_evidence: Time constraints, excessive entry, high workloads, and reduced patient interaction are reported without measured duration.
current_workaround: Offline registers, broad free-text fields, duplicate records, mobile devices, and WhatsApp are reported.
existing_solution: Existing HMIS plus the NCG/KCDO SHIFT and HEALING design frameworks.
contradiction: Usability and workflow alignment may be the root problem, so adding a separate summary tool could increase duplication.
implication: Any candidate must remove a concrete transition or duplicate step inside the existing workflow, not add another destination.
unknowns: Oncology-specific prevalence, exact sites, and whether newer NCG-aligned systems resolve these findings.
provenance_notes: Published primary design-research output; method detail is incomplete.

claim: At Tata Memorial Centre, an EMR-integrated structured retrieval interface reduced mean registry abstraction time from 29.14 to 16.72 minutes, a mean reduction of 12.42 minutes.
source_title: Assessment of an EMR-integrated Onco-Insight hospital-based cancer registry system
supporting_extract: A paired intra-observer comparison reported a 12.42-minute mean reduction with 95% CI 8.99–16.24 and p<0.001; a random sample of 100 cases per cancer system was used.
method_sample: Observational intra-observer comparison by trained registry abstractors using 2021 cases; time compared across 11 cancer systems.
limitations: Registry abstraction is not consultation preparation; one institution and institution-specific EMR; source order was not randomised; 2021 historical data.
frequency_evidence: TMC registered 37,495 cases in 2021 and had 32,359 eligible cancer cases; the timed comparison used sampled cases by cancer system.
burden_evidence: Manual mean 29.14 ± 6.15 minutes versus integrated 16.72 ± 5.03 minutes per case.
current_workaround: Manual navigation and abstraction across institutional EMR modules.
existing_solution: Structured SQL retrieval into one interface with validation and manual review.
contradiction: The demonstrated value comes from structured integration, not generative clinical summarisation.
implication: Structured source retrieval plus human validation has measurable Indian operational value, but consultation transfer is unproven.
unknowns: Whether similar savings apply to clinic preparation, outside records, less integrated hospitals, or unstructured artifacts.
provenance_notes: Exact paired result retained; no cross-workflow extrapolation.

claim: The same Onco-Insight evaluation found high demographic retrieval but only 43.22% automated diagnostic retrieval; follow-up remained fully manual and outside or cross-centre treatment required manual review.
source_title: Assessment of an EMR-integrated Onco-Insight hospital-based cancer registry system
supporting_extract: Of 32,359 confirmed cases, demographic retrieval reached 97.59%, diagnostic retrieval 43.22%, and 52% had complete TMC treatment linked; follow-up and outside-care variables still needed manual work.
method_sample: Observational evaluation of all eligible 2021 registry cases for completeness, with manual validation.
limitations: Institution-specific structured architecture; registry variables differ from consultation needs; article contains some inconsistent summary wording, so exact tables and results were used.
frequency_evidence: Manual review affected outside treatment, cross-centre referral, recurrence/progression treatment, follow-up, and unstructured variables; exact workflow-event rate varies by field.
burden_evidence: Manual work persisted despite integration; field-specific time was not separately reported.
current_workaround: Trained abstractors manually enter unavailable variables and validate retrieved data.
existing_solution: Hybrid structured retrieval with deterministic validation and manual entry.
contradiction: Full automation and a universal summary are not supported; structured completeness and workflow boundaries determine value.
implication: Target explicit source retrieval and review; keep clinical extent, sequence, response, and follow-up interpretation with authorised humans.
unknowns: Which unstructured fields can be safely extracted without clinical interpretation and whether source-linked review is faster.
provenance_notes: Separate bounded claim from the same source; it is not an independent confirmation of EV-0017.

claim: Among 172 responding NCRP-affiliated hospitals, 137 reported a functional tumour board; among those boards, physical documentation dominated, electronic notes and cross-hospital discussion were uncommon, and 48.2% lacked a follow-up system.
source_title: Profiling of tumour board characteristics and functioning for cancer care under hospitals registered under National Cancer Registry Programme in India
supporting_extract: Of 229 invited hospitals, 172 responded. Of 137 boards, 63.5% used physical documentation, 16.8% communicated through EMR notes, 5.1% always conducted cross-hospital discussion, and 48.2% had no recommendation follow-up system.
method_sample: Cross-sectional structured survey in October 2024; 172 hospitals, 75.1% response; mostly registry principal investigators or board nodal staff; descriptive statistics and qualitative coding.
limitations: Self-reported institution-level data; one-month survey; no preparation-time measure or independent audit; NCRP hospitals may not represent all settings.
frequency_evidence: 79.7% of responding hospitals reported a board; 47.4% of boards met weekly and 19% as needed.
burden_evidence: Inadequate documentation and inconsistent follow-up were reported qualitatively; time and labour were not measured.
current_workaround: Physical records, written summaries, direct referring-physician communication, and hybrid documentation.
existing_solution: Local boards, some secretariats, EMR notes, hybrid meetings, and limited cross-hospital review.
contradiction: Tumour boards are already widespread in this hospital segment, so the gap is documentation/follow-up or cross-hospital access—not creation of a generic board.
implication: A narrow board operations wedge has direct India evidence, but a time-saving case-preparation claim remains unmeasured locally.
unknowns: Who prepares cases, person-minutes per case, missing-information causes, and adoption constraints for digital workflow.
provenance_notes: Exact denominators distinguish all respondents from hospitals reporting a board.

claim: NCG already operates a Virtual Tumor Board where member centres submit cases for scheduled cross-centre discussion by oncology experts.
source_title: The Virtual Tumor Board
supporting_extract: The page describes a host-and-centre model, scheduled sessions, 25–30 experts, case submission before meetings, videoconferencing, and a downloadable case template.
method_sample: Official programme page describing current operating model.
limitations: The page may lag operational changes; no participation rate, preparation time, completeness, or outcome evaluation is provided.
frequency_evidence: The page lists recurring Wednesday and Saturday sessions; actual attendance and case throughput were not independently verified.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Case material is submitted to programme coordination and presented through a conferencing workflow.
existing_solution: NCG VTB, recurring expert sessions, a case template, and videoconference infrastructure.
contradiction: A new expert-network or virtual-board product would duplicate an established NCG channel unless it solves a specific access or preparation failure.
implication: Research integration, packet readiness, documentation, or follow-up gaps rather than generic expert connection.
unknowns: Current platform version, case rejection/postponement, data-sharing governance, and preparation burden.
provenance_notes: Contact details from the official page were deliberately excluded.

claim: In a 41-session observational pilot, an integrated tumour-board platform reduced preparation time for oncologists, radiologists, and surgeons, but not pathologists, and did not reduce the number of tasks.
source_title: A New Software Platform to Improve Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Workflows and User Satisfaction: A Pilot Study
supporting_extract: The study recorded 734 tasks across 41 sessions; clinical-course review and other preparation time decreased, while pathology and radiology review time did not change significantly.
method_sample: Paired observational task analysis with two participants from each of four specialties preparing the same breast cases using conventional and NAVIFY methods after training.
limitations: Single institution, breast cases, eight clinicians, fixed method order, and Roche funding/employment conflict; not India-specific.
frequency_evidence: Participants commonly prepared one to six cases per board; small self-reported distribution.
burden_evidence: Most self-reported preparation times exceeded five minutes per case; exact role means were presented graphically, and only significance is retained here.
current_workaround: Separate review of EMR, PACS, LIS, paper notes, screenshots, and presentation files.
existing_solution: Integrated tumour-board platform with source-system links and a longitudinal case view.
contradiction: Pathology and radiology review were not accelerated, and the platform did not remove tasks; integration prerequisites are substantial.
implication: Operational case assembly can be measured by role, but imported time-saving claims require Indian validation and conflict review.
unknowns: Effect in India, in heterogeneous systems, for non-breast cases, and without vendor-sponsored implementation.
provenance_notes: Financial conflict and limited design retained alongside result.

claim: A 495-questionnaire survey found oncologists preferred journals and the internet, and both oncologists and general practitioners wanted rapid access to transparent information.
source_title: Information needs of oncologists, general practitioners and other professionals caring for patients with cancer
supporting_extract: Lack of time was reported by 60% of participants, lack of data by more than 50%, and lack of knowledge by 26% of oncologists; oncologists preferred journals and internet sources.
method_sample: Standardised questionnaire developed with German professional bodies; 495 evaluable questionnaires across cancer-care professionals.
limitations: Germany, 2016, mixed professions, self-report, and no search-time observation; India relevance and current product landscape are uncertain.
frequency_evidence: Survey proportions show reported constraints but not task frequency.
burden_evidence: 60% reported lack of time and more than 50% lack of data as reasons for low consultation confidence; no duration measured.
current_workaround: Congresses, journals, internet, textbooks, and scientific databases.
existing_solution: Existing professional sources and databases.
contradiction: Oncologists reported confidence searching scientific databases, so the gap may be time/access rather than search skill or missing tools.
implication: Find is a real transferable need, but India-specific frequency and differentiation remain weak.
unknowns: Which Indian oncology searches recur and whether source access, licensing, freshness, or workflow causes the burden.
provenance_notes: PubMed abstract used; no unsupported full-text detail.

claim: A 74-response Indian online survey found strong interest in accredited molecular reports and frequent pathologist discussion, while many respondents lacked a molecular tumour board or report-change follow-up.
source_title: Survey for molecular reports in practicing oncologists in India
publisher: International Journal of Molecular and Immuno Oncology
supporting_extract: Among 74 responses, all wanted accredited reports, 82.4% reported reviewing with a molecular pathologist, 68.9% lacked a molecular tumour board, 58.1% reported no information from the reporting team about follow-up or report changes, and 27% did not know an accreditation agency.
method_sample: Anonymised 14-question cross-sectional online survey distributed to hospitals through email and social media from December 2019 to February 2020.
limitations: Small self-selected sample, respondent characteristics intentionally not collected, low/unknown response denominator, confusing wording, and clinical interpretation focus.
frequency_evidence: Practice frequency was not measured; percentages reflect respondent experience/preferences.
burden_evidence: No time or operational burden measurement.
current_workaround: Direct discussion with molecular pathologists and report review.
existing_solution: Accredited laboratories and molecular tumour boards where available.
contradiction: This need is highly specialised and often requires clinical interpretation, so it does not validate a generic record product.
implication: Trust can mean accreditation, source quality, and change communication; operational provenance may help but interpretation stays with specialists.
unknowns: Representative prevalence, current 2026 availability, workflow time, and safe product boundary.
provenance_notes: Publisher page read directly; author contact information was excluded.

claim: An analysis of 1,988 CTRI cancer trials from 2007–2021 found marked cancer-type and state-level disparities, while also documenting incomplete, inconsistent, and non-standard registry fields.
source_title: Landscape of cancer clinical trials in India — a comprehensive analysis of the Clinical Trial Registry-India
publisher: The Lancet Regional Health — Southeast Asia
supporting_extract: The study identified 1,988 trials; among 1,251 treatment trials, 28% were open, 29% not yet recruiting, and 26% completed. Several northeastern and small states had no registered trials, and CTRI field-quality limitations were explicit.
method_sample: Descriptive analysis of CTRI public data downloaded in April 2022; cancer records identified algorithmically and manually checked; state and cancer-burden comparisons.
limitations: Historical registry snapshot, registry status may not equal live site availability, no clinician search observation, and industry-affiliated authors/funding.
frequency_evidence: Trial inventory and geographic availability measured; clinician search frequency not measured.
burden_evidence: Geographic and data-quality gaps shown; search time and referral burden not measured.
current_workaround: CTRI search and manual classification/cross-checking with other registries.
existing_solution: National CTRI registry plus international registries and institutional trial offices.
contradiction: A registry already exists; a new trial finder must solve freshness, data quality, referral, or general discovery without patient-specific matching.
implication: General India trial discovery has evidence, but patient-specific eligibility matching is out of scope and existing-registry differentiation is unresolved.
unknowns: Current data freshness, clinician task frequency, site-contact reliability, and safe non-patient-specific workflow value.
provenance_notes: Exact 2007–2021 study scope retained; no claim that 2022 recruitment status is current.

claim: A prospective cross-sectional study of 172 patients who defaulted at AIIMS Rishikesh found social support, finance, travel, illness, and counselling barriers; the mean journey to the facility was 143 km.
source_title: Factors Associated With Default of Treatment and Follow-Up Among Patients With Cancer
supporting_extract: Among 172 defaulters, reported reasons included lack of social support 26.2%, financial constraints 20.3%, commuting difficulty 16.3%, too ill to attend 13.4%, and more than one reason 16.9%; 59.3% were from outside the state.
method_sample: Prospective study from June 2021 to December 2022; patients defaulting in evaluation, treatment, or follow-up were interviewed in person or by telephone; descriptive analysis.
limitations: Only people who defaulted were sampled, so it does not estimate default prevalence or compare non-defaulters; one centre and mixed reasons.
frequency_evidence: Study enrolled 172 defaults during the period; total eligible denominator and prevalence were not reported.
burden_evidence: Mean travel 143 ± 13.15 km; reason proportions measured, but staff outreach time was not.
current_workaround: Telephone contact, counselling, family support, and travel to a tertiary hub.
existing_solution: Authors discuss counselling and a hub-and-spoke model; intervention effectiveness was not tested.
contradiction: A reminder-only product cannot solve finance, transport, social support, illness, or service distribution.
implication: Continuity is strongly evidenced, but the candidate must support barrier-aware coordination rather than simple reminders or clinical triage.
unknowns: Current outreach workflow, named staff owner, contact completion, baseline follow-up rates, and actionable operational subset.
provenance_notes: Denominator limitation preserved; no causal claim.

claim: In a 206-patient oral-cancer feasibility study, provider SMS prompts generated a 73.68% reply rate but did not eliminate hospital follow-up dropout.
source_title: Short message service prompted mouth self-examination in oral cancer patients as an alternative to frequent hospital-based surveillance
supporting_extract: Of 228 messages, 168 replies were received; 46 message occasions, 20.18%, had no clinician follow-up examination. The authors concluded that SMS improved engagement but did not appear to reduce follow-up dropout.
method_sample: Prospective observational feasibility study at Tata Memorial Centre; 206 adequately treated oral-cancer patients with phone access, 228 prompts sent before scheduled follow-up.
limitations: Selected literate or caregiver-supported population, one cancer and centre, short period, no randomised control, and intervention included clinically oriented self-examination.
frequency_evidence: 228 scheduled follow-up prompts across 206 patients.
burden_evidence: 20.18% of message occasions lacked clinical follow-up despite prompting; staff workload and longer-term attendance were not quantified.
current_workaround: One-way SMS prompting plus standard scheduled clinic visits.
existing_solution: Low-cost SMS reminders and patient education.
contradiction: Digital contact and reply do not equal completed follow-up; reminder-only automation misses structural barriers.
implication: Measure completed operational follow-up and barrier resolution, not messages sent or opened; avoid clinical self-assessment features.
unknowns: Whether two-way coordinator workflows improve attendance and which barriers are actionable by care teams.
provenance_notes: Clinical self-examination result is not promoted; only operational reminder/follow-up evidence retained.

claim: A qualitative study of 100 patients and 48 caregivers at Tata Medical Center Kolkata found multi-provider journeys, uneven access, long-distance travel, referral confusion, communication gaps, and financial disruption across common cancers.
source_title: Journeys: understanding access, affordability and disruptions to cancer care in India
supporting_extract: Six themes covered access journey, psychological experience, stigma, decision-making and adherence, economic cost, and access modifiers; patients often visited several providers before a cancer centre.
method_sample: Cross-sectional qualitative study; stratified purposive sampling to saturation; 100 patients and 48 caregivers across common cancers; in-depth interviews and independent qualitative content analysis.
limitations: Single tertiary charitable centre in eastern India; patient/caregiver rather than care-team workflow; 2017 interviews published in 2022; qualitative findings do not supply prevalence.
frequency_evidence: Repeated themes reached qualitative saturation; population rates were not estimated.
burden_evidence: Travel, repeated providers, cost, communication, and disrupted work/family life were described but not quantified as staff operational time.
current_workaround: Patients and families navigate multiple providers and travel to a tertiary centre.
existing_solution: Local referral, social services, and family support; effectiveness not compared.
contradiction: The largest burden may be access, finance, and navigation rather than clinician record synthesis.
implication: Outside-theme navigation deserves candidate consideration, but the Doctor/Care Team Facing wedge must name an actionable care-team job.
unknowns: Which staff role owns referral readiness, what information is missing, and what can improve without patient-facing clinical advice.
provenance_notes: No participant quotations or identifying case detail copied.

claim: Across 15,653 US oncology physicians and 43.2 million ambulatory visits, weekly EHR time and message volume increased from 2019 to 2022, with medical oncology/haematology carrying the greatest measured burden.
source_title: National trends in oncology specialists’ EHR inbox work, 2019–2022
publisher: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
supporting_extract: Mean weekly EHR time rose from 400.2 to 465.2 minutes, work outside scheduled hours from 189.0 to 211.8 minutes, and messages from 127.4 to 151.6; medical oncology/haematology reached 575.5 EHR minutes per week in April 2022.
method_sample: Longitudinal analysis of deidentified Epic Signal metadata from July 2019 to April 2022; 15,653 oncology physicians, 43,228,633 visits, and multivariable models.
limitations: United States, one EHR vendor, ambulatory physicians only, pandemic-era trend, no direct burnout measure, and not specific to record reconstruction.
frequency_evidence: Weekly activity across 380,879 physician-month observations.
burden_evidence: More than 3.5 hours mean active EHR use outside scheduled work per week in 2022 across oncology physicians.
current_workaround: Physicians and teams process inbox, chart review, documentation, orders, and messages within the EHR.
existing_solution: Team triage, protected time, and AI drafting are discussed; this study did not test a product intervention.
contradiction: EHR burden is real but may be messaging, orders, and documentation rather than fragmented-history preparation.
implication: Do not use international EHR burden as Indian consultation-readiness proof; use it to define measurable workflow components and specialty variation.
unknowns: Comparable Indian audit-log measures and the fraction attributable to record search or reconstruction.
provenance_notes: Exact aggregate metrics retained with geographic transfer warning.

claim: A time-motion study of 97 head-and-neck oncology consultations found EHR tasks consumed a median 44.0% of initial consultation time and 30.7% of follow-up consultation time.
source_title: Quantifying the Electronic Health Record Burden in Head and Neck Cancer Care
supporting_extract: Across 47 initial and 50 follow-up consultations, median EHR time was 19:16 and 03:45 respectively; only 23% of 22 surveyed providers said enough time existed for documentation or timely referral information.
method_sample: Cross-sectional video and screen time-motion study with 12 providers and 97 consultations, plus a validated questionnaire completed by 22 providers.
limitations: Single Netherlands centre and one EHR; head-and-neck specialty; concurrent communication and EHR work; patient satisfaction not measured.
frequency_evidence: Every observed consultation contained EHR work; exact task distribution varied by consultation type.
burden_evidence: 44.0% initial and 30.7% follow-up consultation time; initial consultations averaged 1,664 keystrokes and 593 mouse events.
current_workaround: Providers review, enter, and order inside the EHR during and after consultations.
existing_solution: Existing mature EHR; authors discuss workflow alignment, single data entry, support staff, and optimisation.
contradiction: Information input, not chart review, was the largest measured EHR component in initial consultations; a summary-only product may target the wrong burden.
implication: Measure the exact task before choosing synthesis; documentation or re-entry may dominate in some workflows.
unknowns: Indian task distribution and whether consultation preparation happens before, during, or after the visit.
provenance_notes: Task percentages and consultation counts taken from the primary tables.

claim: Flatiron markets OncoEMR as a specialty oncology EHR with documentation, ordering, billing, operations, mobile access, patient portal, molecular-test integration, staging, templates, reporting, and clinical decision support.
source_title: OncoEMR — Oncology EHR Software
supporting_extract: The product page claims specialty workflows, configurable templates, scheduling, molecular order/result integration, patient access, reporting, NCCN templates, staging, and decision-support functions.
method_sample: Current vendor product page; no independent implementation sample used for this record.
limitations: Vendor claims, US regulatory and reimbursement context, pricing and India availability not established, and many clinical functions are outside hackathon scope.
frequency_evidence: Vendor reports thousands of providers and sites, but figures are not independently verified here.
burden_evidence: No independent burden reduction reported on the page.
current_workaround: Not reported.
existing_solution: Comprehensive specialty oncology EHR category already exists.
contradiction: A generic oncology workspace or EHR is neither novel nor light integration.
implication: Differentiate on one Indian last-mile operational job, not category breadth or clinical functionality.
unknowns: India applicability, cost, integration model, and independent effectiveness.
provenance_notes: All capabilities explicitly labeled vendor claims.

claim: Roche markets navify Clinical Hub as a central tumour-board platform covering meetings, patient lists, case presentations, uploaded reports and images, notes, follow-up, guidelines, publications, trial search, and analytics.
source_title: navify Clinical Hub for Tumor Boards
supporting_extract: The page claims rich patient summaries, report/image access, meeting notes, guideline navigation, search across more than 21 trial registries, patient-specific matching, publication search, and custom reporting.
method_sample: Current vendor product page with links to a vendor-supported prospective study and limited customer survey.
limitations: Vendor positioning, market availability varies, India fit and pricing unknown, and patient-specific guideline/trial functions exceed the hackathon boundary.
frequency_evidence: Not established by the product page.
burden_evidence: Vendor cites a 30% preparation-time reduction from one implementation; independent transfer is not assumed.
current_workaround: Separate case assembly, meeting, source search, and follow-up tools.
existing_solution: Mature commercial end-to-end tumour-board category.
contradiction: A broad tumour-board workspace, case summary, guideline search, and trial matching bundle already exists.
implication: Any Connect candidate needs an India-specific underserved workflow and must omit patient-specific clinical ranking/matching.
unknowns: India availability, interoperability cost, local alternatives, and safe differentiated wedge.
provenance_notes: Vendor claims separated from EV-0021 peer-reviewed but vendor-funded pilot evidence.

claim: HL7 mCODE 4.0 defines oncology-specific FHIR profiles across patient information, disease characterisation, assessment, genomics, treatment, and outcomes.
source_title: HL7 FHIR US mCODE Implementation Guide 4.0.0
supporting_extract: mCODE provides a structured oncology data model and implementation guide but is a US Realm Standard for Trial Use built on US Core.
method_sample: Published HL7 implementation guide.
limitations: US realm, trial-use status, terminology and dependencies are not an India-ready implementation contract.
frequency_evidence: Not applicable to a standard.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Local oncology schemas and manual mapping.
existing_solution: mCODE plus ABDM/FHIR and NCG requirements provide modelling references.
contradiction: A new proprietary oncology schema would duplicate substantial standards work and create mapping burden.
implication: Reuse concepts selectively after workflow selection; do not freeze architecture against a foreign or draft contract now.
unknowns: Mapping to ABDM and NCG modules for the chosen job.
provenance_notes: Realm and trial-use limits retained.

claim: The oncology EHR burden study notes that early evaluations of generative AI reply drafting had not shown substantial reductions in physician inbox time and were unlikely to replace high-performing care teams.
source_title: National trends in oncology specialists’ EHR inbox work, 2019–2022
publisher: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
supporting_extract: The authors point to team triage, workload design, and protected time while warning that early generative reply drafting did not substantially reduce physician EHR inbox time.
method_sample: Interpretation in a national Epic metadata study; the AI evaluations themselves are cited external studies, not the primary measured intervention here.
limitations: Secondary statement, US inbox context, and not a direct evaluation of oncology record summarisation.
frequency_evidence: Not reported for AI use.
burden_evidence: No substantial inbox-time reduction is reported from early evaluations; exact effect belongs to cited intervention studies.
current_workaround: Physician review plus team-based message triage.
existing_solution: Generative draft replies and care-team inbox workflows.
contradiction: Generating text does not necessarily remove review or workflow burden.
implication: Evaluate end-to-end person-minutes and review burden rather than output speed or model quality alone.
unknowns: Whether source-linked extraction for a different workflow reduces total work in India.
provenance_notes: Explicitly treated as secondary evidence within the paper.

claim: The NCG/KCDO Medical Oncology requirements already specify protocol management, dose calculation, interaction checks, toxicity grading, alerts, treatment changes, administration verification, and summaries.
source_title: NCG-KCDO EMR Requirement — Medical Oncology Module v2.0
supporting_extract: The module contains patient-specific protocol, dose, interaction, toxicity, alert, modification, administration, and discharge-summary requirements with doctor and nurse verification.
method_sample: Official requirements developed by an NCG medical-oncology subcommittee; not an adoption study.
limitations: Intended features, not measured implementation, accuracy, usability, or prevalence; most functions are clinically consequential.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Institutional protocols, clinician review, nursing verification, and existing EMR modules.
existing_solution: NCG-aligned medical-oncology EMR requirements explicitly cover the requested Act functions.
contradiction: The theme is not only out of hackathon scope; it is also covered by an existing national oncology EMR direction.
implication: Reject patient-specific Act as a product lane; at most investigate general authentic-source access or clinician-entered documentation separately.
unknowns: Whether a non-patient-specific retrieval burden remains after institutional protocols and existing tools.
provenance_notes: Same source group as EV-0011 but a distinct bounded capability claim; not independent confirmation.

claim: Flatiron markets built-in oncology order templates, staging, precision-medicine workflow, and clinical decision support inside OncoEMR.
source_title: OncoEMR — Oncology EHR Software
supporting_extract: The product page advertises NCCN order templates, AJCC staging, molecular profiling integration, genomic results, and evidence-based treatment decision support.
method_sample: Current vendor product page.
limitations: Vendor claim, US context, no independent effectiveness evidence, and no India fit assessment.
frequency_evidence: Not reported.
burden_evidence: Not reported.
current_workaround: Existing oncology EHR and separate knowledge tools.
existing_solution: Commercial patient-specific oncology decision-support category exists.
contradiction: The requested Act feature bundle is established commercially and directly conflicts with the hackathon exclusions.
implication: Do not pursue this lane; use it only to understand what must remain outside the prototype.
unknowns: Whether general source retrieval can be differentiated safely in India.
provenance_notes: Same vendor source group as EV-0030; not independent confirmation.

setting: National Cancer Grid Virtual Tumor Board
claim: The current public NCG VTB page describes a host-and-centre model, deadline-based case submission, scheduled videoconference discussion, and a downloadable presentation template, but does not describe a public post-meeting decision handoff or follow-through process.
source_title: The Virtual Tumor Board (VTB)
supporting_extract: Member centres submit cases before recurring Wednesday or Saturday sessions; host centres run sessions and experts contribute. The page provides participation, submission, hosting, equipment, schedule, and template information, but no public post-meeting workflow.
method_sample: Direct review of the current official programme page.
limitations: The page may lag actual operating practice; absence of public documentation is not proof that no internal decision or follow-up process exists.
frequency_evidence: Recurring Wednesday and Saturday sessions are listed; case throughput is not reported.
burden_evidence: Submission deadlines imply coordination but no person-time, rejection, postponement, or follow-through burden is measured.
current_workaround: Case presentation is submitted to programme coordination and discussed by videoconference under a host-centre model.
existing_solution: NCG VTB provides recurring sessions, expert participation, coordination, and a presentation template.
contradiction: The existing national programme already solves scheduling and access to a board; a new generic board would duplicate it.
implication: Investigate only a specific post-meeting operational handoff and never infer non-existence from undocumented public pages.
unknowns: Actual post-meeting decision record, recipient, responsible actor, assignment, acknowledgement, due state, and completion tracking.
provenance_notes: Public contact details and clinical case examples were deliberately excluded; same source group as EV-0020, not independent confirmation.

setting: National Cancer Grid Virtual Tumor Board
claim: The public NCG VTB presentation template structures presenter and centre information, diagnosis, brief presentation and examination, treatment history, investigations, imaging, treatment fitness where relevant, and questions for the board; it contains no visible decision, owner, due-date, communication, or completion fields.
source_title: NCG Virtual Tumor Board presentation template
supporting_extract: The six-slide blank template ends with questions for the tumour board after brief history, investigations, imaging, and fitness sections.
method_sample: Direct extraction of the public blank PowerPoint template; six slides reviewed.
limitations: A presentation template may be only one part of the workflow and may intentionally omit internal minutes, EMR entries, or post-meeting systems.
frequency_evidence: Template is linked for recurring VTB submission; actual usage and completion rates are not reported.
burden_evidence: No preparation time, missing-field rate, or rejection rate is reported.
current_workaround: Presenters prepare a slide deck using the published template.
existing_solution: A standardised public case-presentation artifact already exists.
contradiction: Pre-board structure is not absent; novelty must come from an evidenced handoff rather than recreating the case form.
implication: Treat the template as a possible input boundary, not a product to replace; seek the separate human decision and operational disposition artifacts.
unknowns: Whether a decision/minutes template exists privately, who authors it, who receives it, and how actions are tracked.
provenance_notes: No filled case, patient data, presenter name, centre name, or contact detail was collected.

claim: iECHO participant guidance describes invitation-based case upload into a selected session, programme-team review, approval or rejection, and re-upload after a stated rejection reason.
source_title: Submitting a case presentation
supporting_extract: The participant follows a hub invitation, selects the participant group and session Content area, uploads a file, and waits for programme-team approval or rejection; rejected submissions can be corrected and re-uploaded after email or SMS notice.
method_sample: Direct browser review of the public iECHO participant help article.
limitations: Generic iECHO guidance, not an NCG-specific usage audit; it documents pre-session content handling and says nothing about post-board decisions.
frequency_evidence: No NCG case count, rejection rate, or turnaround is reported.
burden_evidence: Revision loop exists but no frequency or time burden is reported.
current_workaround: Invitation, session-specific file upload, review, rejection reason, notification, and re-upload.
existing_solution: iECHO already supplies a review-state workflow for pre-session case content.
contradiction: A basic upload, review, and notification product would duplicate the current platform.
implication: Do not rebuild pre-board file review; test whether the post-board decision-to-action handoff is outside this documented workflow.
unknowns: NCG configuration, decision capture, post-session distribution, action assignment, outcome tracking, and retention rules.
provenance_notes: Page content was read through a browser because static extraction returned only the hosting shell; no account or private programme was accessed.

claim: iECHO hub guidance assigns the organisation team responsibility for choosing case presenters, reviewing uploaded content, checking for PII or PHI, approving or rejecting it, and sharing approved content with participants.
source_title: How to add a Case presenter
supporting_extract: The organisation team assigns active participants as presenters; the platform notifies them, keeps uploads under review, supports download and approve or reject, sends a rejection reason, and shares approved files. The guidance recommends PHI and PII review.
method_sample: Direct browser review of the public iECHO hub help article.
limitations: Generic platform documentation, not evidence that NCG uses every feature or that the organisation team owns post-board actions.
frequency_evidence: Multiple presenters are supported; usage rates are not reported.
burden_evidence: No review time, rejection rate, privacy incident rate, or workload measure is reported.
current_workaround: Organisation or programme staff administer presenter assignment and content approval in iECHO.
existing_solution: A pre-board operational owner, review states, notifications, privacy check, and controlled sharing already exist in the platform.
contradiction: The pre-board actor and review workflow are clearer than the post-board problem; Candidate B should not bundle both without evidence.
implication: Treat the organisation/programme team as a known pre-board actor only; keep the post-board owner unresolved.
unknowns: Which NCG role performs this work, whether the same role records decisions, and what happens after the session ends.
provenance_notes: Same iECHO help source group as EV-0038; public guidance only, with no user account or patient content.

subproblem: NCG VTB operating roles and platform migration
setting: National Cancer Grid Virtual Tumor Board
workflow_moment: case intake review scheduling and presentation
claim: An NCG 2022 programme account says participants submitted weekly case presentations to an ECHO-appointed coordinator working with NCG experts, disease-management groups reviewed presentations before spokes presented, and VTBs moved to iECHO to streamline scheduling and produce more programme metrics.
source_title: NCG Newsletter Issue 4 — Virtual Tumor Board activity
supporting_extract: The programme account identifies a coordinator, expert review, disease-site groups, invited presentation, videoconference operation, and an October 2022 migration to iECHO for streamlined scheduling and more programme metrics.
method_sample: Direct review of the official NCG newsletter feature describing programme operations through 2022.
limitations: Historical programme description; named contacts and current platform configuration may have changed; post-meeting decision ownership is not described.
frequency_evidence: The source describes weekly submissions and recurring programmes, with historical attendance summaries but no current throughput retained here.
burden_evidence: No coordinator time, review delay, rejection rate, or action-follow-up measure is reported.
current_workaround: Coordinator intake, NCG expert and disease-group review, invited presentation, and iECHO-supported sessions.
existing_solution: NCG and ECHO India already provide programme coordination, review, scheduling, and platform operations.
contradiction: National coordination and pre-board review are established; the unmet step must be narrower and current.
implication: Coordinator is evidenced for pre-board intake, not post-board accountability; verify current roles before naming a product user.
unknowns: Current coordinator arrangement, post-meeting decision artifact, treating-team acknowledgement, action assignment, and outcome visibility.
provenance_notes: Public personal contact details in the newsletter were not copied; this source does not independently prove current practice.

subproblem: formal MDT coordinator role transfer evidence
workflow_moment: meeting preparation minutes distribution and pathway follow-through
claim: A formal NHS regional guideline assigns an MDT coordinator responsibility for meeting coordination, advance lists and evidence, attendance and minutes, distributing notes, producing agreed action plans and reviews, recording data, monitoring milestones, and escalating delays.
source_title: Policy and Guidelines for Investigation, Diagnosis and Management of Malignancy of Unknown Origin and Cancer of Unknown Primary
publisher: NHS England West Midlands Clinical Networks
supporting_extract: The coordinator duties include preparing patient lists and evidence, taking and distributing minutes, ensuring diagnoses and plans enter notes, producing action plans with agreed reviews, monitoring milestones, reporting, and escalating delays.
method_sample: Official regional policy for a specific NHS cancer pathway; responsibilities section reviewed directly.
limitations: England, CUP-specific, published in 2018 and expired for local review in 2018; role design cannot be assumed for Indian boards.
frequency_evidence: Defines recurring role responsibilities but reports no workload frequency.
burden_evidence: No time, caseload, or effect size is reported.
current_workaround: A dedicated coordinator maintains meeting artifacts, communication, action plans, pathway data, and escalation.
existing_solution: Formal coordinator-led MDT operations demonstrate that decision-to-action ownership is an established workflow pattern elsewhere.
contradiction: This evidence may describe a staffing and governance function rather than a software gap, and cannot name the Indian owner.
implication: Use coordinator as a role hypothesis and interview target, not as an India-specific fact or automatic product user.
unknowns: Whether Indian hospitals assign equivalent duties, whether one person owns them, and which tasks are unmet versus manually adequate.
provenance_notes: No patient, staff contact, or local identifier retained; geographic and currency limits are explicit.

workflow_moment: case selection scheduling review attendance and decision documentation
claim: A draft NABH oncology HIS/EMR annexure specifies tumour-board patient selection, unique board ID, scheduling, clinician notifications, a central case list, integrated record review, attendance, and documentation of multidisciplinary inputs, recommendations, and follow-ups; it does not specify an operational acknowledgement, action owner, due date, or intermediate completion state.
source_title: NABH Digital Health Standards for HIS EMR Systems — Annexure for Cancer Care and Management
publisher: National Accreditation Board for Hospitals & Healthcare Providers
supporting_extract: MDC 1(a) requires patient selection, tumour-board ID assignment, review scheduling, and clinician notifications; 1(b) describes a central scheduled-patient view; 1(c) records attendance; 1(d) documents multidisciplinary diagnosis, treatment-recommendation, and follow-up inputs in a standardised summary.
method_sample: Draft Indian digital-health certification annexure for oncology HIS/EMR systems; its multidisciplinary-care section defines four tumour-board objective elements.
limitations: Draft status and publication date are not stated in the document; requirements are not evidence of implementation or burden. The referenced sample summary is marked as annexure XXX. Clinical recommendation content exceeds this project's product boundary.
frequency_evidence: No frequency or adoption measurement is reported.
burden_evidence: No person-time, delay, missing-data, acknowledgement, or completion baseline is reported.
current_workaround: Not measured; the annexure describes intended HIS/EMR capability rather than current local practice.
existing_solution: NABH's draft standard already defines a substantial electronic tumour-board workflow and overlaps NCG/KCDO requirements.
contradiction: Weakens novelty for a broad tumour-board module and shows that public standards already expect scheduling, integrated review, attendance, and decision/follow-up documentation; it does not establish the proposed intermediate handoff gap.
implication: Validate only the narrow post-decision acknowledgement and operational-status handoff against actual implementations; do not recreate the standard's broad board workflow.
unknowns: Whether the draft was finalised or implemented; whether certified systems capture acknowledgement, owner, due date, and completion; how follow-up is defined locally.
provenance_notes: Direct reading of the public NABH-hosted draft PDF on 2026-09-03; clinical recommendation text is retained only to describe the standard and is not promoted as product scope.

subproblem: single-centre post-board spreadsheet and coordinator workflow
workflow_moment: weekly case listing decision entry and post-board treatment follow-up collection
claim: A one-year Eastern India tumour-board audit used preformed Excel case lists, entered the board's management decision after each meeting, and used a patient care coordinator to collect later treatment and follow-up information, trace unreachable patients, and complete a master chart.
source_title: Incorporation of a Multidisciplinary Tumor Board in Cancer Patient Care: Experiences of a Comprehensive Cancer Care Hospital in Eastern India
publisher: Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Care
supporting_extract: The weekly board prepared case lists beforehand on preformed Excel sheets; after the meeting the recommended management plan was entered. Treatment details and follow-up data were then collected from hospital records with help from a patient care coordinator, who attempted to trace patients and complete the master chart.
method_sample: Prospective before-and-after data collection for a 12-month single-centre audit, August 2020 to July 2021; 800 case discussions, including 573 new cases and 227 repeat discussions.
limitations: Single private hospital; audit workflow may not represent routine operations elsewhere. The study measures treatment and follow-up data completeness, not treating-unit acknowledgement, coordinator person-time, or product effectiveness. More than 20% of some data remained missing.
frequency_evidence: The board met weekly and recorded 800 discussions in 12 months; 28.37% were repeat discussions.
burden_evidence: The audit reports 20.75% unknown treatment status, 31.5% lost to follow-up at analysis, and 20.37% missing staging data, but no staff person-time or decision-acknowledgement rate.
current_workaround: Preformed Excel case list and master chart, repeated checking, hospital-record review, and patient care coordinator tracing.
existing_solution: A named patient care coordinator plus spreadsheet-based board register and follow-up collection operated at this hospital.
contradiction: Provides one direct Indian actor and post-board workflow, showing that staffing and a spreadsheet may already own the task; however substantial missing and unknown data persisted. It does not prove a decision-to-treating-unit acknowledgement gap.
implication: The patient care coordinator is a plausible operator in some hospitals. P5 should test whether the initial job is decision entry, treating-unit acknowledgement, or later data collection, and whether a lightweight improvement removes rather than duplicates the spreadsheet.
unknowns: Who entered the board decision; whether the treating unit acknowledged it; which fields existed in the preformed sheet; coordinator time; reasons for missing data; current workflow after the 2020–2021 audit.
provenance_notes: Direct reading of the journal landing page and full article PDF on 2026-09-03. No patient-level data or author contact details were retained.
